# How to Draft a Gracious Resignation Letter with Claude in 10 Minutes

> **In short:** Claude can draft a short, kind resignation letter in under 10 minutes when you give it clear context about your role, your reason for leaving, and the tone you want. The result is a starting draft you'll edit yourself — Claude can't know your workplace politics, so it can't be the final word.

A resignation letter is one of those small professional tasks that can feel much bigger than it is. You're emotional, time is short, and you want to leave on good terms without sounding fake or overly apologetic. Claude is good at this exact kind of writing: a short, structured note where warmth matters more than cleverness. Here's how to do it from scratch, even if you've never used Claude before.

## Before you start
- A free Claude account at **claude.ai** (sign-up takes about a minute with an email address).
- A browser or the Claude mobile app — both work the same way for this task.
- A rough idea of three things: your job title, how long you've been there, and why you're leaving (one line is enough).
- About **10 minutes** of quiet time. The free plan is enough; a paid plan just gives you more messages per day.

## Step 1 — Open Claude and start a fresh chat
Go to **claude.ai** in your browser, or open the Claude app on your phone. If you don't already have an account, you'll be prompted to create one with your email — it takes about a minute. Once you're signed in, look for a button or icon that says "New Chat" or shows a **plus sign (+)** — it's usually at the top of the sidebar on the left. Click or tap it. A blank conversation opens with a message box at the bottom. This empty chat matters: it tells Claude that everything you type over the next few minutes belongs to this one task, so it won't get tangled up with anything else you've asked about. If you can't find the new-chat button, look for a pencil icon or "Start new conversation" instead — different versions of the app place it in slightly different spots.

💬 Example: type a short greeting like "Hi Claude" to confirm the chat is responding.

You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a blinking cursor, ready for your first instruction.

## Step 2 — Tell Claude the basics
Now type a short paragraph explaining your situation. Imagine you're briefing a thoughtful friend who knows nothing about your job. Include four things: your **job title**, how long you've been in the role, the kind of place you work (small team, large company, school, hospital), and a one-line reason for leaving. Don't worry about writing it perfectly — Claude is good at pulling key facts out of messy notes. Press Enter or tap the send arrow when you're done, and Claude will start replying within a second or two. If your screen looks different on a tablet or older app version, you might see a **paper-airplane icon** instead of an arrow — both do the same thing.

💬 Example: "I'm a marketing coordinator at a mid-size nonprofit. I've been here three years. I just accepted a role at another organization. I want to leave on good terms."

You'll know it worked when Claude acknowledges your situation and either asks a short follow-up or starts planning the letter.

## Step 3 — Ask for a draft with a specific tone
Now ask Claude to write the actual letter. Be specific about the **length** and the **feeling** you want. A short, clear instruction works better than a long one. Tell Claude how long the letter should be — around **150 words** is a sweet spot for most resignation letters: long enough to feel polite, short enough that your manager will actually read it. Also describe the mood: warm, grateful, professional, brief. If there's a specific phrase you want included, like thanking a manager by name, mention it here. Claude writes the draft in the same chat, so the context from Step 2 is automatically in mind. If nothing appears within about 20 seconds, click the send button again — sometimes the first tap doesn't register on a slow connection.

💬 Example: "Please draft a resignation letter of about 150 words. Tone: warm, grateful, professional. Two weeks' notice. Please thank my manager Sarah for her mentorship. Do not name my new employer."

You'll know it worked when Claude produces a complete, well-structured letter you can read straight through.

## Step 4 — Refine the tone until it sounds like you
Read the draft **out loud**, in your own voice. Does it sound like something you'd actually say to your boss? Most first drafts from Claude are polite but a touch generic — they can read like they were written by a very well-mannered robot. If a sentence feels too stiff, too formal, or just not-quite-you, type a short note asking Claude to fix that one part. Phrases like "make this warmer" or "loosen up the opening" work well. Claude will rewrite only the part you flagged, leaving the rest of the letter intact. This back-and-forth is normal — two or three small tweaks usually turn a generic draft into something that sounds honest. Keep your feedback short and specific rather than rewriting whole paragraphs yourself.

💬 Example: "The second paragraph feels too formal. Can you make it warmer and more like how I'd actually talk to a manager I've worked with for years?"

You'll know it worked when you read the new version and quietly think, "Yes — that sounds like me on a good day."

## Step 5 — Personalize the small details
Now fill in the blanks Claude couldn't fill for you: the exact date, your manager's correct title, the specific projects or moments you want to thank them for, and your last working day. These small, real details are what turn a polite letter into a meaningful one. Type them into the chat and ask Claude to slot them into the right places. Be explicit about anything you want to leave out — for example, if you don't want your new employer's name mentioned, say so. Keep in mind that Claude can draft a kind letter, but it doesn't know the unspoken politics of your workplace, so for sensitive situations — a tough boss, a tricky reason for leaving — trust your own judgment over the AI's suggestions.

💬 Example: "Please add: my last day will be Friday, 14 March. In the thank-you paragraph, mention that I'll always be grateful they trusted me with the annual fundraiser."

You'll know it worked when the letter contains your real dates, names, and one specific detail that only you could have written.

## Step 6 — Copy the letter into your own document
Once the letter sounds right, click and drag to select Claude's final draft, then copy it (Ctrl+C on Windows, Cmd+C on Mac, or long-press on a phone). Open your email, Word, or Google Docs — whatever you'll actually send from — and paste it in. Read it one last time on your own, without Claude's interface in the way. Reading in a different place helps you spot small errors Claude may have introduced, like a wrong name or an odd word choice. Make any final edits by hand. When you're happy, save or send. If your workplace prefers a quick email to a formal attachment, you can also ask Claude to give you a shorter, four-sentence version in the same chat — it'll keep the tone consistent.

💬 Example: "Can you also give me a 4-sentence email version of the same letter, suitable for sending as a quick message?"

You'll know it worked when you have a saved file or sent message that reads naturally, sounds like you, and feels kind — ready to deliver.

## Common mistakes
- **Skipping the context.** Jumping straight to "Write me a resignation letter" with no info about your role, tenure, or reason gives Claude nothing to work with. The result sounds like a template you could have Googled. **Fix:** spend 60 seconds on Step 2, even if your notes are messy.
- **Asking Claude to sound "really apologetic."** Claude mirrors your tone. If you ask for guilt, the letter reads guilty. Aim for grateful and professional instead — that's what most managers actually want to hear. **Fix:** replace "apologetic" with "warm and grateful" in your prompt.
- **Forgetting to say what to leave out.** Claude will happily mention your new employer, your salary, or your real feelings about the job unless you tell it not to. **Fix:** be explicit ("Please don't name my new employer" or "Keep the reason for leaving vague").
- **Copy-pasting without reading aloud.** Typos, wrong names, and odd phrases slip past when you skim silently on a phone screen. **Fix:** read the whole letter once, out loud, before sending.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Most of us will leave a job at some point. Knowing how to draft a quick, kind resignation note is a small life skill that pays off when emotions are running high and you don't want to write from a blank page.
- **For your business or work:** The same prompt pattern — context, tone, short refinement, personalize, send — works for almost any professional message: a thank-you note after an interview, a polite decline to a vendor, a short apology to a client.
- **If you're just getting started:** The fastest first move is to open Claude and ask it to draft *any* short message, even a personal one. You'll learn the rhythm of the back-and-forth without pressure, and the same steps will feel easy the next time you need them.

## Try it now
Open Claude and paste this single sentence into a new chat: *"Draft a 150-word resignation letter. I'm a teacher at a small primary school, leaving after five years for a role closer to home. Tone: warm, grateful, not over-apologetic."* Read the result out loud, then change one sentence to sound more like you. That's the whole skill — ten minutes, one honest letter, done.
